text:
HELMER (with the letters in his hand). Look here. See how they have piled up. (leafing through them.) What is this?

NORA (at the window). The letter! Oh no, no, Torvald!

HELMER. Two calling cards—from Rank.

NORA. From Doctor Rank?

HELMER (looking at them). Doctor of Medicine Rank. They were on top; he must have slipped them in when he left.

NORA. Is there anything written on them?

HELMER. There is a black cross above the name. Look here. It is a rather uncanny idea. It is exactly as though he were announcing his own death.

NORA. That is what he is doing.

HELMER. What? Do you know something? Has he told you anything?

NORA. Yes. When those cards arrive, he has taken leave of us. He intends to shut himself in and die.

HELMER. My poor friend. I knew, of course, that I would not be allowed to keep him for long. But so soon—. And then he hides himself away like a wounded animal.

NORA. When it has to happen, it is best that it happen without words. Is that not so, Torvald?

HELMER (paces up and down). He was so closely bound up with us. I do not think I can imagine him gone. He, with his sufferings and his loneliness, gave, as it were, a clouded background to our sunlit happiness.—Well, perhaps it is best this way. For him, at any rate. (stops.) And perhaps for us too, Nora. Now the two of us are left entirely to each other alone. (puts his arms around her.) Oh, my beloved wife; I do not think I can hold you tightly enough. Do you know, Nora—many a time I wish that some imminent danger might threaten you, so that I could risk life and blood and everything for your sake.

NORA (tears herself free and says loudly and resolutely). Now you shall read your letters, Torvald.

HELMER. No, no, not tonight. I want to be with you, my beloved wife.

NORA. With the thought of your friend’s death—?

HELMER. You are right. This has shaken us both; something ugly has come between us; thoughts of death and dissolution. We must seek release from this. Until then—. We will each go our own way.

NORA (with her arms around his neck). Torvald—good night! Good night!

HELMER (kisses her on the forehead). Good night, my little songbird. Sleep well, Nora. Now I shall read through the letters. (he takes the bundle into his room and closes the door behind him.)

NORA (with wild eyes, gropes about, seizes Helmer’s domino, wraps it around herself, and whispers rapidly, hoarsely, and brokenly:) Never see him again. Never. Never. (throws her shawl over her head.) Never see the children again either. Not them either. Never; never.—Oh, the ice-cold black water. Oh, the bottomless—; this—. Oh, if only it were over.—Now he has it; now he is reading it. Oh no, no; not yet. Torvald, farewell, you and the children—

(She is about to rush out through the hall; at that same moment Helmer tears open his door and stands there with an opened letter in his hand.)

HELMER. Nora!

NORA (screams loudly). Ah—!

HELMER. What is this? Do you know what is written in this letter?

NORA. Yes, I know. Let me go! Let me get out!

HELMER (holds her back). Where are you going?

NORA (tries to tear herself free). You must not save me, Torvald!

HELMER (reels backward). True! Is what he writes true? Terrible! No, no; it is impossible that this can be true.

NORA. It is true. I have loved you above everything in the whole world.

HELMER. Oh, do not come to me with foolish evasions.

NORA (takes a step toward him). Torvald—!

HELMER. You wretched woman—what have you done!

NORA. Let me go away. You must not bear it for my sake. You must not take it upon yourself.

HELMER. No playacting. (locks the hall door.) You will remain here and answer to me. Do you understand what you have done? Answer me! Do you understand it?

NORA (looks steadily at him and says with an expression that is growing rigid:) Yes, now I am beginning to understand it to the very bottom.

HELMER (paces about the floor). Oh, what a terrible awakening this is. During all these eight years—she who was my joy and pride—a hypocrite, a liar—worse, worse—a criminal!—Oh, the bottomless ugliness that lies in all this! Shame, shame!

NORA (remains silent and continues to look steadily at him).

HELMER (stops in front of her). I should have suspected that something like this would happen. I should have foreseen it. All your father’s frivolous principles.—Be silent! You have inherited all your father’s frivolous principles. No religion, no morality, no sense of duty—. Oh, how I have been punished for turning a blind eye to him. I did it for your sake; and this is how you repay me.

NORA. Yes, this is how.

HELMER. Now you have destroyed all my happiness. You have ruined my entire future for me. Oh, it is terrible to think of. I am in the power of an unscrupulous man; he can do with me whatever he pleases, demand anything at all of me, order and command me as he sees fit—and I dare not make a sound. And I must sink so miserably and be ruined because of a frivolous woman!

NORA. When I am no longer in this world, then you will be free.

HELMER. Oh, no theatrics. Your father always had such phrases ready to hand too. What good would it do me if you were no longer in this world, as you say? It would not do me the slightest good. He could still make the matter public; and if he does, I may perhaps be suspected of having known about your criminal act. People may perhaps think that I was behind it—that it was I who urged you on! And I have you to thank for all this—you, whom I have borne upon my hands throughout our entire marriage. Do you understand now what you have done to me?

NORA (with cold calm). Yes.

HELMER. This is so incredible that I cannot grasp it. But we must try to settle matters. Take off the shawl. Take it off, I tell you! I must try to satisfy him in one way or another. The matter must be hushed up at any cost.—And as for you and me, it must appear as though everything between us were just as before. But naturally only in the eyes of the world. You will therefore continue to remain here in the house; that goes without saying. But you will not be allowed to bring up the children; I dare not entrust them to you—. Oh, to have to say this to her whom I have loved so deeply, and whom I still—! Well, it must be over. From this day forward, it is no longer a question of happiness; it is only a question of saving the remains, the fragments, the appearance. (the entrance bell rings.)

HELMER (starts). What is that? So late. Could the most terrible thing—! Could he—! Hide yourself, Nora! Say you are ill.
